arXiv:2505.02072v1 [cs.CL] 04 May 2025

What do Language Model Probabilities Represent?
From Distribution Estimation to Response Prediction

Eitan Wagner    Omri Abend Affiliation: Hebrew University of Jerusalem Email: {first_name}.{last_name}@mail.huji.ac.il
Abstract

The notion of language modeling has gradually shifted in recent years from a distribution over finite-length strings to general-purpose prediction models for textual inputs and outputs, following appropriate alignment phases. This paper analyzes the distinction between distribution estimation and response prediction in the context of LLMs, and their often conflicting goals. We examine the training phases of LLMs, which include pretraining, in-context learning, and preference tuning, and also the common use cases for their output probabilities, which include completion probabilities and explicit probabilities as output. We argue that the different settings lead to three distinct intended output distributions. We demonstrate that NLP works often assume that these distributions should be similar, which leads to misinterpretations of their experimental findings. Our work sets firmer formal foundations for the interpretation of LLMs, which will inform ongoing work on the interpretation and use of LLMs’ induced distributions.

1 Introduction

Language modeling was originally defined as a probability distribution over finite sequences of tokens from a given vocabulary Shannon (1948); Bahl et al. (1983). With the rise of Large Language Models (LLMs), the common use of these models has shifted Rogers and Luccioni (2024). In the original sense, the primary use was distribution estimation: the goal was to output a probability distribution pθp_{\theta} that matches the language’s data-generating distribution. Recently, however, these models have been used for response prediction instead: the goal is to output “correct” responses to queries Chung et al. (2022); Brown et al. (2020). Towards the goal of making such systems better, recent models additionally undergo reward-based tuning (Ziegler et al., 2020, e.g., RLHF;) to align their responses with human preferences.

As models typically output probabilities over the next token, we argue that it is important to assess how the shift in usage affects the expected output probabilities. Consider, for example, a simple scenario with a biased coin with p⁡(H)>0.5p(H)>0.5 (see Fig. 1). Simple completion of a sentence, indicating the outcome, may reflect biases in the training data.11 1 See Gupta et al. (2025), who show that models are generally biased towards heads, even when prompted that the coin is fair, as this is predominant in the training data. We describe this case as distribution estimation of the source distribution, which, in this case, is identical to traditional language modeling. In contrast, a user may wish for the true p⁡(H)p(H): the probabilities of the underlying world events. We describe this case as target distribution estimation. For the language modeling distribution to coincide with the distribution of world events, the training data must consist solely of faithful reports of events according to their world distribution, which is not the scenario that we usually encounter.

A user may also wish for a model to output a prediction about the unobserved outcome, where accuracy is the objective. In this case, the output distribution will be inherently different, as accuracy is maximized when the entire mass is on the mode (i.e., p⁡(H)=1p(H)=1). Indeed, attempting to calibrate the model with the data-generating distribution will lower the accuracy of prediction. We refer to this case as response prediction. This output distribution is expected when the model’s objective considers the mode only and not the rest of the distribution. This is also expected if the data distribution itself reports predictions, even if the model is trained for standard language modeling. This can happen when the input is an instruction and the completion is a prediction (which should maximize accuracy).

In this paper, we analyze possible intended interpretations of the output probabilities of LMs and their relationship to training and inference strategies. We formally define the distinctions between the tasks of source distribution estimation, target distribution estimation, and response prediction (§ 2). We discuss different training and inference settings for LMs (§ 3) and how different settings are appropriate for different use cases (§ 4). We analyze how different inference strategies affect the expected output distributions (§ 5). We show that many works implicitly assume equality between the distributions in the different use cases, thereby positing unwarranted claims (§ 6). We conclude with a call for caution when relying on probabilistic interpretations of LLM outputs (§ 7).

2 Background: Distribution Estimation and Response Prediction

In this section, we provide formal definitions for distribution estimation, prediction, and event distribution prediction. Here we address the general case, and the following sections will relate these definitions to common language tasks.

2.1 Distribution Estimation

The statistical task of distribution estimation involves constructing a distribution that approximates an unknown data-generating (or “source”) distribution, based on a set of observed samples (Wasserman, 2013).

More formally, in the conditional case, let pS​(y∣x)p_{S}(y\mid x) be a conditional source distribution we wish to estimate, where x∈𝓧x\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}} denotes an input and y∈𝓨y\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}} denotes an output. The task of distribution estimation is to learn, based on observed data S={(xn,yn)}n=1NS=\{(x_{n},y_{n})\}_{n=1}^{N} sampled from pSp_{S}, a mapping: pθ:𝓧→Δ|𝓨|−1p_{\theta}:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}\to\Delta^{|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}|-1}. The resulting distribution estimator pθ(⋅∣x)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) is an approximation of pSp_{S}.

Distribution estimators are typically fit to minimize the cross-entropy (or, equivalently, the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence), from the empirical distribution of the data:

argminθ∑(xi,yi)∈S−logpθ(yi∣xi)\displaystyle\argmin_{\theta}\sum_{(x_{i},y_{i})\in S}-\log p_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x_{i}) (1)

In the optimal case, we get a model for which pθ(⋅∣x)=pS(⋅∣x)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)=p_{S}(\cdot\mid x), which completely recovers the data-generating distribution. We describe this as an ideal estimator and denote it by pθ∗p_{\theta^{*}}.

Target distribution estimation.

In some cases, we intend to estimate a distribution pTp_{\text{T}} which is not identical to the source distribution, pSp_{S}, from which the data is sampled. We call this target distribution estimation. The process in which the data from pSp_{S} is used for improving a task over pTp_{\text{T}} is sometimes referred to as transfer learning Weiss et al. (2016).

A simple case is when pSp_{S} generates biased or corrupted samples of pTp_{\text{T}} Crammer et al. (2005). Knowing the relationship between the distributions allows us to learn about pTp_{\text{T}} with data from pSp_{S}.

2.2 Response Prediction

As opposed to distribution estimation, response prediction is a task of returning a single output y∈𝓨y\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}} for a given input x∈𝓧x\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}. We thus define a predictor as a function fθ:𝓧→𝓨f_{\theta}:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}, which we attempt to learn fθf_{\theta} based on the data SS (Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, 2014).22 2 A special case of response prediction, in which 𝓨\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}} is a finite set, is also known as classification.

The goal of prediction models is typically to minimize the expected loss defined for the output predictions, e.g., the misclassification error.

We define a decision function fdecf_{\mathrm{dec}} as a function from a distribution to a target fdec:Δ|𝓨|−1→𝓨f_{\mathrm{dec}}:\Delta^{|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}|-1}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}. Predictors sometimes consist of a decision function on top of a learned distribution Bishop and Nasrabadi (2006). That is, we have fθ=fdec∘pθf_{\theta}=f_{\mathrm{dec}}\circ p_{\theta}.

Example: Consider the ideal model pθ∗p_{\theta^{*}} and the decision function fdec=argmaxf_{\mathrm{dec}}=\text{argmax}. The resulting predictor fθf_{\theta} is known as the Bayes optimal classifier and is proved to be the one that minimizes the misclassification error, with respect to the distribution pSp_{S} Devroye et al. (2013).

Given a dataset {(xm,ym)}m=1M∼pS\{(x_{m},y_{m})\}_{m=1}^{M}\sim p_{S}, the predicted set {(xm,fθ​(xm))}m=1M\{(x_{m},f_{\theta}(x_{m}))\}_{m=1}^{M} can reflect a different distribution. For example, if fθf_{\theta} is a deterministic function (e.g., a Bayes optimal classifier), the conditional entropy will be 00, which might not be the case in the original data. If, instead, a model randomly samples based on pθ∗p_{\theta^{*}}, then the original and predicted sets will follow the same distribution, and the entropy will be similar.

We note that target distribution estimation can be formalized as a prediction task, where the output space is the distributions Δ|𝓨|−1\Delta^{|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}|-1}, possibly rounded for discretization. This task can therefore be performed by applying a decision over possible distributions in Δ|𝓨|−1\Delta^{|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}|-1}.

3 Praxis: LM Training and Inference

In this section, we describe common training and inference strategies used in contemporary language models. For each strategy, we analyze its probabilistic interpretation. We show that chosen strategies directly impact the plausible interpretation of model outputs.

3.1 Probabilistic Language Modeling

A language model is traditionally defined as a distribution over finite strings Shannon (1948); Bahl et al. (1983). Formally, let 𝒱\mathcal{V} be a language model’s vocabulary, composed of (sub)words w∈𝒱w\in\mathcal{V}. A language model is then a distribution p⁡(𝐰)p(\mathbf{w}), where 𝐰∈𝒱∗\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{V}^{*} is a sequence of words. Typically, language modeling is achieved through a next-word prediction model, which allows us to write the distribution autoregressively as:

p⁡(𝐰)=∏t=1|𝐰|p⁡(wt∣𝐰<t)\displaystyle p(\mathbf{w})=\prod_{t=1}^{|\mathbf{w}|}p(w_{t}\mid\mathbf{w}_{<t}) (2)

Next-word prediction and language modeling are almost equivalent, except for a pathological case where next-word prediction gives infinite sequences a positive probability, which is disallowed by the traditional definition. Du et al. (2023) derive theoretical criteria for language models that avoid this case and show that common models fulfill these criteria.

A language model also defines the conditional distribution:

p⁡(𝐰𝚢∣𝐰𝚡)=∏t=1|𝐰𝚢|p⁡(wt𝚢∣𝐰𝚡∘𝐰<t𝚢)\displaystyle p(\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}}\mid\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}})=\prod_{t=1}^{|\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}}|}p(w^{\mathtt{y}}_{t}\mid\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}\circ\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}}_{<t}) (3)

where 𝐰𝚡,𝐰𝚢∈𝒱∗\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}},\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}}\in\mathcal{V}^{*} are sequences of words, respectively representing the context input to the model and the model’s output, ∘\circ is the concatenation function, and p⁡(𝐰𝚡)>0p(\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}})>0.

We denote an ideal language model, i.e., one that perfectly models the data distribution, by pLMp_{\text{LM}}.

3.2 Training Stages

Most modern language models go through a multi-stage training procedure. We follow Touvron et al. (2023); Groeneveld et al. (2024) in describing these stages here (see Fig. 2).

T1. Pretraining.

The first stage of fitting a language model is typically termed pre-training, and consists, in short, of distribution estimation. Let pLMp_{\text{LM}} be a language model we wish to approximate, and {𝐰n}n=1N\{\mathbf{w}^{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} be a large set of strings sampled from it. We can consider each of these strings’ time steps to define an input-output pair: (wtn,𝐰<tn)(w^{n}_{t},\mathbf{w}^{n}_{<t}). We then train a distribution estimator pθp_{\theta} to fit this language, minimizing its cross-entropy on this data (as in § 2.1). Given a trained model pθp_{\theta} , we can then use it as either an unconditional or conditional language model (i.e., using eq. 2 or eq. 3).

T2. Adaptation/Fine-tuning:

  1. 1.

    Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): Modern models are explicitly finetuned to follow instructions Zhang et al. (2024c); Touvron et al. (2023); Groeneveld et al. (2024).

    The datasets comprise instruction-following examples Chung et al. (2022); Wang et al. (2023b); Wang et al. (2023a). We term the set of possible instructions as the input space 𝓧\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}} and the set of possible responses as the output space 𝓨\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}. The distribution of responses presp_{\text{res}} is not necessarily the same as the empirical distribution of the pretraining data, since it was constructed to include only helpful responses.

    As in pretraining, supervised instruction-tuning is done with a cross-entropy loss. The goal is to optimize θ\theta to minimize the average cross-entropy over full responses

    argminθ1j∑i=1j−logpθ(yi∣x∘y:i−1))\displaystyle\argmin_{\theta}\frac{1}{j}\sum_{i=1}^{j}-\log p_{\theta}(y_{i}\mid x\circ{y}_{:i-1})) (4)

    The optimization is performed for query+response pairs sampled from presp_{\text{res}}.

  2. 2.

    Human preferences. A common additional step is training the model to align with human preferences. This is typically done with a trained reward model, which is trained using human feedback on outputs from the model Ziegler et al. (2020); Chaudhari et al. (2024).

    Here θ\theta is optimized to maximize the reward function, r:𝓨×𝓧→ℝr:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}\times\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}\to\mathbb{R}, representing the return of an output yy for an input xx. In the simple setting, the reward is maximized by a model that places all the mass on the response with the highest reward. In practice, a modified reward function is used, in which a term is added to penalize a distribution that is far from the one resulting from pretraining.

3.3 Inference

As described in § 1, many language model users these days care about some referent events of interest and not about the probabilities of specific strings. For example, given some specific context, we might care about the probability of the world event that a coin will land on heads. We might not care about the probability of a specific string used to describe this event, e.g., `​`​the coin landed on heads′′``\texttt{the coin landed on heads}^{\prime\prime}, which also encompasses the wording choices.

We denote an output string by 𝐰𝚢∈𝒱∗\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}}\in\mathcal{V}^{*} and we define its corresponding referent event by y∈𝓨y\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}. Since the model outputs strings and their probabilities, different strategies are necessarily applied to map models’ output probabilities to the probabilities Δ𝓨−1\Delta^{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}-1} of the referents. We define a mapping ϕ:𝒱∗→𝓨\phi:\mathcal{V}^{*}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}} from string outputs to their referent event. We note that a single referent event may be mapped to by many different strings, i.e., for y1=y2∈𝓨y_{1}=y_{2}\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}, it is possible that 𝐰𝚢1≠𝐰𝚢2\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}_{1}}\neq\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}_{2}}.

In the coin-toss example, we can use 𝓨={heads,tails,×}\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}=\{\texttt{heads},\texttt{tails},\times\}, where ×\times denotes an invalid response. ϕ\phi maps all verbal responses to 𝓨\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}.

To obtain referent event probabilities we consider two general methods: logit probabilities and explicit probability report (see Fig. 3):

I1. Logit probabilities:

We assign probabilities to the answers based on their generation probability. This is the distribution from which the actual output can be sampled.

For the input, we consider the following formats:

  1. 1.

    Naïve completion: In this option, we simply input a prompt and look at the generation probabilities of the completion. Mapping each possible completion to a relevant output by ϕ\phi will give a legal distribution over 𝓨\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}.

    Formally, we define the näive completion probability as

    pNC(y∣𝐰𝚡)≔∑𝐰∈𝒱∗pLM(𝐰∣𝐰𝚡) 1{ϕ(𝐰)=y}\displaystyle p_{\text{NC}}(y\mid\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}})\coloneqq\sum_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{V}^{*}}p_{\text{LM}}(\mathbf{w}\mid\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}})\,\mathbbm{1}_{\{\phi(\mathbf{w})=y\}} (5)

    For example, if xx is the sentence “Paris is the capital of”, then the probability is the sum of the generation probabilities of all strings that map to “France”.

  2. 2.

    Zero-shot instruction: Radford et al. (2019) show that pretraining alone gives models some capacity for many tasks. This capability is termed zero-shot transfer. By inputting an appropriate instruction prompt, the completion can be treated as a response.

    Formally, we define an instruction I⁡(𝐰𝚡)\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}) as a transformation that takes a prompt 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} and formats it as an instruction.

    In our example, if 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} is the sentence “Paris is the capital of”, I⁡(𝐰𝚡)\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}) can be something like:
    “Q: What country is Paris the capital of? A: ”.

    The zero-shot instruction probability is defined as

    pZS​(y∣𝐰𝚡)≔\displaystyle p_{\text{ZS}}(y\mid\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}})\coloneqq
    ∑𝐰∈𝒱∗pLM(𝐰∣I(𝐰𝚡)) 1{ϕ(𝐰)=y}\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{V}^{*}}p_{\text{LM}}(\mathbf{w}\mid\mathrm{I}(\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}))\,\mathbbm{1}_{\{\phi(\mathbf{w})=y\}} (6)
  3. 3.

    Few-shot instruction: Brown et al. (2020) further show that generative language models are highly capable of following instructions based on a few examples. This method is also known as few-shot (in-context) learning, as it only adds context and does not perform explicit training. In this case, the query is preceded with a few examples of queries with expected responses.

    Similar to zero-shot instructions, we define a few-shot instruction FS⁡(𝐰𝚡)\mathrm{FS}(\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}) as a transformation that takes a prompt 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} and formats it as an instruction with a few examples.

    In the current example, FS⁡(𝐰𝚡)\mathrm{FS}(\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}) can be something like:
    “Q: What country is Madrid the capital of? A: Spain.
    Q: What country is Washington DC the capital of? A: USA.
    Q: What country is Paris the capital of? A:     ”.

    The few-shot instruction probability is thus

    pFS​(y∣𝐰𝚡)≔\displaystyle p_{\text{FS}}(y\mid\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}})\coloneqq
    ∑𝐰∈𝒱∗pLM(𝐰∣FS(𝐰𝚡)) 1{ϕ(𝐰)=y}\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{V}^{*}}p_{\text{LM}}(\mathbf{w}\mid\mathrm{FS}(\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}))\,\mathbbm{1}_{\{\phi(\mathbf{w})=y\}} (7)

I2. Explicit probability report:

Rather than using the output probabilities of the model to obtain response probabilities, it is possible to instruct the model, possibly with few-shot examples, to explicitly report probabilities of different options. In the multiple-choice example, this is done by instructing the model to generate a list of probabilities corresponding to the options.

Notably, unlike logit probabilities, this method does not explicitly force a legal distribution (e.g., that all possibilities sum up to 11) as the output.

4 Use Cases for the Different Strategies

In the previous section, we described different training and inference strategies. Theoretically, all combinations between the training and inference strategies we defined are possible. However, depending on the task, an inference strategy must be used, and training should be chosen accordingly. Here we describe different use cases of language models and their appropriate inference and training strategies.

4.1 Text completion

A common use of language models is to randomly generate text to complete a prompt 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}. Assuming we want the text to be similar to human-written text, a continuation 𝐰𝚢\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}} should appear according to the ideal language modeling distribution pLMp_{\text{LM}}. An example where this type of distribution is desired is story generation, where we want a model to continue a story in original ways. This is a case that uses a distribution learned during source distribution estimation (2.1)

The intended output distribution is naïve completion pNCp_{\text{NC}} (item 1) as the completion does not directly follow an instruction, and only pretraining (§ 3.2) is required.

4.2 Response generation

Perhaps the most common use of modern language models is for creating a response 𝐰𝚢\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}} to a query 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}, e.g., in question-answering. In this case, the main concern is the quality of the response, in terms of truthfulness and avoiding harm, and scores are assigned accordingly. The rational choice, for optimal response quality, is to always generate the response with the highest score.33 3 In reality, humans tend to add randomness to their choices, even in prediction cases. The strategies by which people choose are investigated in prospect theory Vulkan (2000); Shanks et al. (2002).

This is a case of response prediction (2.2). Since this case involves formatting the question as an instruction, inference should use the zero-shot distribution pZSp_{\text{ZS}} (item 2) or, preferably, the few-shot distribution pFSp_{\text{FS}} (item 3). Training for instructions (items 1 and 2) will be beneficial.

4.3 Event modeling

In some cases, we might care about world events and their probabilities. This can happen when a response or completion refers to world events and we want an unbiased answer. In this case, we look at the event distribution pE​(y∣x)p_{\text{E}}(y\mid x), for x∈𝓧x\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}} corresponding to text input 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} and y∈𝓨y\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}} corresponding to a possible text output 𝐰𝚢\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}}. This is a case of target distribution estimation (2.1)

Using instruction-based inference (i.e., pZSp_{\text{ZS}} or pFSp_{\text{FS}}) with a question about the resulting event will give a distribution reflecting the choice of the optimal response, which is generally not the true world-event distribution. Using pNCp_{\text{NC}} without an instruction should match the language modeling distribution, and will reflect the world-event distribution only if the language modeling distribution is unbiased. Setting aside some toy settings, this is not the case in general. For example, Paik et al. (2021) show that language models are biased towards describing bananas as green, presumably since yellow bananas are commonly described without their color.

Another option is explicit probability reports (3.3), which, if successful, can obtain unbiased probabilities. This method is highly dependent on the quality of the model as it requires inference about a distribution other than the training data. Therefore, in practice, extensive adaptation training is used (items 1 and 2).

5 Analysis: Prompts and their Ideal Output Distributions

In this section, we propose a formal framework for analyzing the generation process of textual responses. We start with some definitions and move to address three cases that correspond to different data-generating distributions, represented by three ideal conditional language models. Our analysis shows how different input prompts can lead to different ideal output distributions.

5.1 Definitions

We use the term ground for the set of propositions that are considered true Green (2021). This includes both propositions that were explicitly stated and propositions that are stipulated, based on common knowledge or some inference process.

The text is assumed to be generated by an agent, which we describe on the basis of the belief-desire-intention (BDI) framework Bratman (1987). Beliefs are the agent’s knowledge, desires are its general goals, and intentions are specific plans for actions, based on the beliefs and desires.

We use the following (simplified) setting: we are given an input string 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} which sets the ground. We consider possible output strings 𝐰𝚢\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}}, which are assumed to be generated by some agent. The beliefs and desires of the agent can be established from the ground. We define the agent’s beliefs as a set of events b𝚢={yn}b^{\mathtt{y}}=\{y_{n}\} and its desire d𝚢d^{\mathtt{y}} as a random variable ff, drawn from a space of functions from beliefs to strings D𝚢={fn},fn:b𝚢→𝒱∗D^{\mathtt{y}}=\{f_{n}\},\,f_{n}:b^{\mathtt{y}}\to\mathcal{V}^{*}. p⁡(f∣𝐰𝚡)p(f\mid\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}) describes the probability of applying the function ff given the ground 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}.

We further assume here that 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} includes a reference to some world event, denoted by xx, in addition to other possible information, and that 𝐰𝚢\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}} has a unique referent event yy.

  • In the coin toss example, 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} states a coin toss event xx and also possibly adds information, such as whether the outcome y∈{heads,tails}y\in\{\texttt{heads},\texttt{tails}\} was observed. The agent generates a response about yy based on its beliefs b𝚢b^{\mathtt{y}}, which include the knowledge of what happened, and its desires D𝚢D^{\mathtt{y}}, which, for example, can include faithfully reporting what it observed or accurately predicting what it did not observe.

5.2 Case 1: Multiple Descriptions of an Outcome

In the simple case, we consider a set of possible output strings 𝐰1𝚢,…​𝐰k𝚢\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}}_{1},\dots\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}}_{k} that refer to the same event yy. Additionally, we consider an input prompt 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} that is not formatted as an instruction, thus no explicit desire is imposed.

  • For example, the possible strings can be different ways to describe the coin landing on heads, like “The coin landed on Heads” and just “Heads”.

Here, different output probabilities reflect different manners of expression. If the ground 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} does not impose restrictions, the LM should reflect the frequency of use. This aligns with the original language modeling definition, which was used to model statistical patterns in language usage Shannon (1951).

5.3 Case 2: Observed Outcome

A different situation is when we consider possible responses that refer to different outcomes. For simplicity, we assume that 𝐰𝚢\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}} is the only way to express yy. We also assume that 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} contains, possibly implicitly, an instruction I⁡(x)\mathrm{I}(x) for the agent.

How does the probability pLM​(𝐰𝚢∣𝐰𝚡)p_{\text{LM}}(\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}}\mid\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}) relate to pE​(y∣x)p_{\text{E}}(y\mid x)? This depends on whether the agent observes the outcome 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} according to the ground.

Assume the agent observes the outcome, i.e., 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} states that y∈b𝚢y\in b^{\mathtt{y}}, and that it always faithfully reports that outcome, i.e., d𝚢={f(y)=𝐰𝚢}d^{\mathtt{y}}=\{f(y)=\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}}\}. In this case, we get

pLM​(𝐰𝚢∣𝐰𝚡)=pE​(y∣x)\displaystyle p_{\text{LM}}(\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}}\mid\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}})=p_{\text{E}}(y\mid x) (8)

If the agent does not always faithfully report yy, the resulting distribution may be biased. This occurs in many practical scenarios, such as when the agent assumes yy to be obvious (e.g., the banana is yellow), when the agent is deceptive, or when the agent has noisy observations. Therefore, in practice, we cannot assume pLMp_{\text{LM}} reflects an unbiased event distribution.

  • In the coin example, 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} states that a coin was tossed and an agent saw the outcome. If 𝐰𝚢\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{y}} states that the agent always reports the outcome then the resulting distribution will reflect the coin bias. Otherwise, a reporting bias might be added.

5.4 Case 3: Unobserved Outcome

A different case is when the agent has no knowledge of whether the event yy happened or not (according to the ground 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}). In this case, 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} can include an instruction to the agent, implying that it must make a prediction. The predictors that the agent can apply are those in D𝚢D^{\mathtt{y}}.

  • In the coin example, 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} states that a coin was tossed and an agent that did not see the outcome is asked to predict what happened.

We can write:

p(y∣x;𝐰𝚡)=∑f∈D𝚢p(f∣𝐰𝚡) 1{f(x)=y}\displaystyle p(y\mid x\,;\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}})=\sum_{f\in D^{\mathtt{y}}}p(f\mid\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}})\,\mathbbm{1}_{\{f(x)=y\}} (9)

Assume the agent knows the event probability of the outcome (e.g., the coin’s bias). I.e., 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} implies that p⁡(y)∈b𝚢p(y)\in b^{\mathtt{y}}. In this case, the only rational behavior by the agent is to use a predictor ff that selects the most likely outcome yy with probability 1.

Controlling the prediction function.

How can we affect the distribution in which the agent selects a predictor p⁡(f∣𝐰𝚡)p(f\mid\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}})? This can be done either by training the agent or by setting the ground.

We write p⁡(f∣𝐰𝚡)∝p⁡(f)⋅p⁡(𝐰𝚡∣f)p(f\mid\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}})\propto p(f)\cdot p(\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}\mid f). This shows three possible ways to affect the choice of the predictor:

  1. 1.

    Training the prior probability p⁡(f)p(f). This is the approach in agent-based training, such as RLHF (see item 2).

  2. 2.

    Training the conditional probability p⁡(fθ∣𝐰𝚡)p(f_{\theta}\mid\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}), for an appropriate input string. This is the approach in supervised fine-tuning for instructions (see item 1).

  3. 3.

    Changing the ground so as to affect the probability. This can be done by raising the likelihood of this prompt given the predictor p⁡(𝐰𝚡∣f)p(\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}\mid f). An example of this is few-shot in-context learning (item 3), where 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} includes example responses attributed to the responding agent. Replacing I⁡(x)\mathrm{I}(x) with FS⁡(x)\mathrm{FS}(x) will raise the probability of a predictor ff that follows the examples.

6 Common Misconceptions

In the previous sections, we identified three possible intended distributions for LM outputs: completion distribution, response distribution, and event distribution. Here we argue that confusion between these interpretations leads to some misconceptions. We also show that clarifying this difference can explain hitherto unexplained results in the literature in some cases. In other cases we find that the difference between these definitions was overlooked, leading to unwarranted claims.

We note that these works also have many merits and contain meaningful experiments which we do not discuss. Our goal is to demonstrate how the formalization of the different interpretations of the LM output distributions can inform the ongoing discussion in NLP, uncover misconceptions, and suggest ways of understanding empirical findings.

6.1 Completion distribution ≠\neq Response distribution.

Consider the following prompts, as in Hu and Levy (2023):

  • (a) “The keys to the cabinet”
    (b) “Here is a sentence: The keys to the cabinet... What word is most likely to come next?”

and consider the probability of the next word being “is” or ”are”.

Despite the apparent similarity, the probabilities are essentially different: p⁡(are∣prompt (a))p(\text{are}\mid\text{prompt (a)}) comes from the completion distribution which is a distribution estimation task, whereas p⁡(are∣prompt (b))p(\text{are}\mid\text{prompt (b)}) comes from the response distribution, which is a prediction task. While p⁡(are∣prompt (a))p(\text{are}\mid\text{prompt (a)}) should be similar to the frequency in the training data, p⁡(are∣prompt (b))p(\text{are}\mid\text{prompt (b)}) should be close to 11 if the completion “are” is the most frequent in the data.

Therefore, there is no reason to assume that the probabilities with prompt (a) will be the same as with (b). However, making this assumption is not rare. For example, Hu and Levy (2023) compare the quality of predictions in these two cases, explicitly assuming that a model that perfectly performs the metalinguistic task (prompt (b)) should have an identical probability distribution over the next word given in the simple completion task (prompt (a)). Their findings about a performance gap should therefore not be interpreted as a deficiency of the LM, but rather as an inherent discrepancy between the two distributions. Similarly, Wagner et al. (2024) design tests for consistency of span distributions by comparing equivalent factorizations of the joint probability. The factorization involves masked language modeling (MLM), which, for autoregressive models, is estimated using a prompt instructing to fill in a missing word. As MLM is a distribution estimation task (like prompt (a)) and instruction-following is a prediction task (like prompt (b)), equating the terms is unwarranted. Here too, their results that show different trends are expected.

Whereas in the previous examples, prediction probabilities are assumed to behave like distribution estimations, the opposite also occurs. For example, Holtzman et al. (2020) discuss the curious phenomenon that text generated by the highest likelihood tends to have low quality. As Meister et al. (2022) note, selecting the highest likelihood yields predictable strings with substantially less information than the distribution over natural strings. Arguably, text generation by highest likelihood treats language generation as a response prediction task, ignoring the fact that text completion is a task that should use distribution estimation (see § 4.1).

Notably, the distinction here is analogous to the difference between language modeling and Shannon’s guessing game, which was used for estimating language entropy in Shannon (1951). Some works address the game as equivalent to autoregressive language modeling (Zouhar et al., 2024, e.g.,), ignoring the predictive nature of the game. See Appendix A for more details.

6.2 Response distribution ≠\neq Event distribution.

Consider the following question and answers, as in Yona et al. (2024):

  • (Q) “When was Mark Bils born?”
    (A1) “March 22, 1958.”
    (A2) “I think he was born on March 22, 1958, but I’m not sure.”

The answer (A1) is worded more conclusively than the answer (A2). Assume the model M1M_{1} generates (A1) and the model M2M_{2} generates (A2), given the question (Q). Should we expect pM1​(A1∣Q)p_{M_{1}}(\text{A1}\mid\text{Q}), when the other option is an answer with a different birth date, to be significantly higher than pM1​(A1∣Q)p_{M_{1}}(\text{A1}\mid\text{Q}), reflecting the difference in confidence? not necessarily. If the objective is accuracy, then both models should always generate the same birth date as long as there is no better option. The level of confidence in the answer reflects the probability of the answer being correct, which is a reported event distribution, whereas the generation probability reflects what the model should output, which follows a response distribution.

This distinction was sometimes overlooked. For example, Yona et al. (2024) compare the decisiveness in a model’s response, to its intrinsic confidence, which is the generation probability. They identify gaps and conclude that LLMs are poor at faithfully conveying uncertainty. As we argue that generation probabilities should not be interpreted as confidence scores, the resulting gap is unsurprising and the aforementioned conclusion is unwarranted. Similarly, Liu et al. (2023) investigate the gap between output probabilities with a query and internal probing probabilities. Here too, response probabilities are assumed to ideally match the correctness probability.

Another case of this distinction is regarding calibration. Consider a question for which a model outputs an answer aa with confidence p>0.5p>0.5. The model is said to be calibrated if the probability of aa being correct equals pp Guo et al. (2017). Does this mean the LM should generate the answer aa with frequency pp? If the objective is accuracy, the LM should always generate aa, and the generation probability should be larger than pp. In other words, the level of confidence need not affect the chosen behavior, as long as there is no better option.

However, many works address calibration of generative LMs by assessing the generation probabilities, assuming the probabilities should ideally reflect confidence. For example, Kalai and Vempala (2024) derive a lower bound on the hallucination rate for calibrated models, with the assumption that calibration is appropriate in the generation setting. In another example, Zhang et al. (2024b) explicitly assume that fitting answers that appear more frequently in the corpus should elicit calibration. Many other works Jiang et al. (2021); Zhu et al. (2023); Dhuliawala et al. (2022) treat the, possibly normalized, output probabilities as confidence scores. The general finding in these papers, that LMs are poorly calibrated and that instruction tuning hurts calibration, is therefore not surprising.

6.3 Completion distribution ≠\neq Event distribution.

Consider the following question and the possible distributions of answers:44 4 The belief distribution is based on a survey of American grown-ups in 2022. See https://carsey.unh.edu/publication/conspiracy-vs-science-survey-us-public-beliefs

  • (Q) “Is Earth flat or round?”
    (D1) 80%80\%: “Earth is round”;
    10%10\%: “Earth is flat”;
    10%10\%: “I’m not sure”;
    (D2) 100%100\%: “The majority of the population believes that earth is round. Despite the scientific evidence supporting this belief, a nonnegligible part of the population believes earth is flat.”

Given the question (Q), should a model generate answers based on the distribution (D1) or based on (D2)? this depends on the objective. If a model intends to reflect an average person, then distribution (D1) should be used, but if the model attempts to respond with the most accurate answer then (D2) should be given. Notice that if a model generates by (D1) then in approximately 10%10\% of the interactions, the model would argue, possibly in a completely confident manner, that earth is flat. This example shows that the distribution of what is said, as in the language distribution, does not necessarily coincide with the distribution of correctness, as in the event distribution. This distinction is related to David Hume’s “is-ought problem” Schurz (2013).

Some works overlook this distinction, implicitly equating the two distributions. For example, Sorensen et al. (2024) discuss three types of pluralism in language model generations. The third is distributional pluralism, in which the generated answers reflect the distribution of positions in the population. This is problematic as it implies that any position (that was not ruled out) can be randomly generated confidently.55 5 The paper mentions an opposite limitation – that distributional pluralism gives higher probabilities to more frequent positions. This concern possibly prioritizes the goal of diversity over accuracy.

In contrast, Lake et al. (2024) show how RLHF models shift from distribution pluralism to Overton pluralism, where the model tends to aggregate all the relevant information in a single response. This is in line with our interpretation of the task as prediction, in which we expect the model to give a high probability to a single best answer.

The previous examples deal with cases in which the model has access to information that explicitly addresses and refutes a common belief (fact-checking). A similar argument can be made for the case of multiple judgments. Consider a case where multiple independent judges are prompted with an identical question, and some answer aa is generated with proportion p>0.5p>0.5. If mistakes behave like white noise, the correctness probability of the majority vote will increase with the number of judges, with a probability that goes to 11 McLennan (1998), thus in this case, pp underestimates the correct probability. This phenomenon is known as “wisdom of the crowd” and is relevant to some domains but not others Kuncheva et al. (2003). 66 6 See Zhang et al. (2024a) for analysis of different types of disagreement between human labels and the effect of a majority vote.

Some work ignored this domain dependence. For example, Baan et al. (2022) posit that a model that assigns probabilities by the proportion of annotator labels should be perfectly calibrated by definition. This assumes equivalence between judgment and correctness, ignoring the nature of the task. Similarly, Meister et al. (2025) construct a benchmark for testing the alignment between an LLM’s output distributions and human variation, assuming this is requested.77 7 This paper also measures the output distribution based on the logit outputs, thus confusing response probabilities with correctness probabilities (§ 6.2).

7 Discussion and Conclusion

In reinforcement learning techniques such as RLHF, LLMs are interpreted as agents in a Markov Decision Process (MDP) with textual states and actions Ziegler et al. (2020). Li et al. (2024) discuss how the application of RLHF shifts LLMs from world models to agents. They address the resulting behavior as a practical way to promote planning (especially with long outputs) while hurting modeling. More generally, some works discuss the phenomenon in which training with SFT or RLHF leads to a lack of diversity, or “mode collapse” O’Mahony et al. (2024).

Our analysis shows the crucial role of the inference method in this behavior. Formatting a prompt as a question creates a conditional distribution in which mode collapse may actually reflect the data generation distribution. We show that in many cases, we are simply modeling a specific situation in which the data itself exhibits high confidence.

As naïve sampling from an autoregressive model was found to be of low quality Holtzman et al. (2020), many sampling methods for generation were proposed. Meister et al. (2023) formalized these methods as sampling adapters, which are transformations of the distribution for generation purposes. Tan et al. (2024) interpret the effect of RLHF in light of this framework. Our analysis shows that common inference methods inherently lead to a transformation or the output distribution.

Our analysis reveals, that among the three common uses of LMs outlined in this paper, explicit reporting seems to be the only one that is aligned in its goals with obtaining event probabilities. This comes with practical challenges, as expressing a distribution in words limits the ability to report complex distributions. Additionally, LLMs suffer from unwanted biases, such as by the order of choices (Zheng et al., 2024). Methods for mitigating these challenges are thus crucial for the robust application of LLMs for world modeling.

In this work, we described three different interpretations of their output probabilities, guided by different user goals. The importance of the presented discussion is underscored by the sizable body of previous work that has unwarrantedly equated them. As some works interpret LM through their probabilistic nature (Geva et al., 2022, e.g., ), our work calls for caution in terms of the interpretation of model probabilities in different contexts.

Limitations

In this work, we assumed there is an underlying persistent distribution that language modeling (pre)training tries to capture. This assumption simplifies the analysis but is probably an oversimplification, as language is dynamic and highly complex. Also, our analysis of the generation process uses many simplifying assumptions. Real-world scenarios are significantly more complex, but we do believe that the general principles we discuss are still relevant.

This work studies the formalization and theoretical aspects of language tasks, thus often simplifying them. Therefore, the categorization into three general distributions is coarse and does not cover all the delicate details of language tasks.

We also note that our discussions of existing work are based on our understanding and it is possible that we misinterpreted them.

Appendix A Shannon’s Guessing Game

In his famous work, Shannon (1948) estimated the entropy and redundancy of the English language, implicitly defining the language modeling distribution. Shannon (1951) further derived empirical bounds for the entropy of the English language through a guessing game. In one version of the game, a person is randomly given texts with a previous (limited) context and is instructed to guess what the next letter is. The guesser continues guessing until they guess the correct letter, and the number of attempts is recorded. Based on his results, Shannon derived upper and lower bounds on English.

Despite the similarity between the guessing game and language modeling, they are fundamentally different in their objectives: language modeling is an estimation task. The goal is to represent the probabilities of occurrence of sequences of words or characters in natural language. In Shannon’s guessing game, on the other hand, the goal is to give an optimal prediction of the real character and not to estimate its probability. The guesser is assumed to always choose the highest ranking character in the distribution. For this reason, the results from the game were used to derive bounds and not for direct estimation.

Works that address the game as an autoregressive language modeling (Zouhar et al., 2024, e.g.,) ignore the predictive nature of the game, thus confusing a completion distribution with a response distribution (see 6.1).

We also note that it is also incorrect to assume that the ranking in a prediction task is equivalent to Shannon’s game. While Shannon assumes the guesser to guess based on the rank in some implicit language modeling, the probabilities of a prediction model have no guarantees beyond the identity of the highest-ranking prediction.

Glossary

0-1 loss:

Also called misclassification rate Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David (2014). This is the expected number (given a target distribution and a predictor) of incorrect predictions. The misclassification rate is closely connected to accuracy, which is the expected number of correct predictions.

Calibration:

Calibration is a measure of the quality of the output confidence of a model. A model is said to be fully calibrated if, for any 0≤p≤10\leq p\leq 1, the expected proportion of correct predictions in the set of predictions with confidence pp is exactly pp Guo et al. (2017). In practice, predictions are binned by confidence intervals, and approximate calibration scores are measured.

Conditional Distribution:

We denote the conditional distribution of YY given XX by pY|Xp_{Y\mid X}. Since we only deal with conditional distributions of this sort, we simply use pp. It is common to use the notation p⁡(y∣x)≔pY|X​(x,y)p(y\mid x)\coloneqq p_{Y|X}(x,y).

Confidence:

In addition to a specific output y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, a predictor can output an estimated probability pp for yy being the correct output. pp is called the confidence score.

Decision function

We define a decision function fdecf_{\mathrm{dec}} as a function from a distribution to a target fdec:Δ|𝓨|−1→𝓨f_{\mathrm{dec}}:\Delta^{|\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}|-1}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}.

Distribution estimation:

The task of approximating a (conditional) distribution pSp_{S}. This is an application of density estimation to discrete random variables.

Distributional divergence:

This includes all functions that measure distances or divergences between probability distributions. These include proper distance functions, such as Total-variation distance and JS-divergence, and also measures like JS- and KL- divergence and cross-entropy Tsybakov (2008). These measures are minimized when the two compared distributions are identical.

Ground:

We use the term ground for the set of propositions that are considered true Green (2021). The ground can be set in an input prompt 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}}.

Ideal estimator:

A model that perfectly represents the source distribution. This means the distributional divergence between pθp_{\theta} and pSp_{S} is minimal. Ideal estimation is generally unattainable but can serve as a proxy for the intended behavior.

Input variable:

We denote an input random variable by XX, with possible values x∈𝓧x\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}.

Language modeling:

A language model is traditionally defined as a distribution over finite strings Shannon (1948); Bahl et al. (1983). Formally, let 𝒱\mathcal{V} be a language model’s vocabulary, composed of (sub)words w∈𝒱w\in\mathcal{V}. A language model is then a distribution p⁡(𝐰)p(\mathbf{w}), where 𝐰∈𝒱∗\mathbf{w}\in\mathcal{V}^{*} is a sequence of words.

Output variable:

We denote an output random variable with YY, with possible values y∈𝓨y\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}.

Predictor:

This is simply a function fθ:𝓧→𝓨f_{\theta}:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}\to\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}. A predicted value fθ​(x)f_{\theta}(x) is called a prediction.

Referent Event:

A referent event is an occurrence in the world to which an utterance refers. We denote the event referred to by an utterance 𝐰𝚡\mathbf{w}^{\mathtt{x}} by xx.

Response prediction:

This is the task of outputting a value y∈𝓨y\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}, given an input x∈𝓧x\in\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}} (Shalev-Shwartz and Ben-David, 2014). When 𝓨\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}} is a discrete, finite set, this task is often called classification.

Reward function:

A reward function (or simply a reward) is a function r:𝓧×𝓨→ℝr:\boldsymbol{\mathcal{X}}\times\boldsymbol{\mathcal{Y}}\to\mathbb{R} representing the return of an output yy for an input xx. Here too, we define rx​(y)≔r⁡(x,y)r_{x}(y)\coloneqq r(x,y). In many cases, a modified reward function is used, in which a term is added to penalize a distribution that is far from the one resulting from pretraining.

Source distribution:

the (conditional) distribution from which training data is generated. We denote this by pSp_{S}.

Target distribution estimation:

Target distribution estimation is the task of estimating a distribution pTp_{\text{T}} which is not identical to the source distribution, pSp_{S}, from which the data is sampled.
